Oldbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Sandwell and the Black Country
s1loc: Oldbury sits at the heart of Sandwell, where the visitor draw is the industrial story of the Black Country. The Black Country Living Museum at nearby Dudley pulls big crowds to its costumed streets and underground mine, while Forge Mill Farm at West Bromwich keeps families coming for its rare breeds and farm trail. The medieval Bromwich Hall and the late-Victorian Haden Hill House Museum anchor the heritage end of the borough's offer.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Sandwell Valley Country Park, a wide green space with walking and cycling trails, a working farm and the Sandwell Valley Visitor Centre courtyard. Barnford Park sits near the town centre with its play areas and games courts, Langley Park hosts community events, and the Rowley Hills, the highest landform in the Black Country, give walkers panoramic views across the region and beyond.

Heritage and culture carry the canal age into the present. The Galton Valley Canal Heritage Centre at Smethwick tells the story of the Birmingham Canal Navigations, while Titford Pool and the Titford Canal, the highest navigable point on the network, draw boaters and towpath walkers. Lightwoods House and Park at Bearwood, recently restored with its landscaped gardens, hosts exhibitions and events through the warmer season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel cluster strung along the M5 at Junction 2, with the Premier Inn, Travelodge, Holiday Inn Express and Ibis Styles serving business and stopover trade close to the Hawthorns. Sandwell and Dudley and Smethwick Galton Bridge stations and the motorway network bring day-trippers in for football fixtures, the canals and Birmingham's attractions, so operators here handle visitor flow across the year.

Irvine.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Ayrshire coast
s1loc: Irvine carries a maritime visitor economy on the North Ayrshire coast, anchored by the Scottish Maritime Museum on the harbourside. The museum's Linthouse Building, Scotland's Cathedral of Engineering, is a Victorian glass-roofed hall of 1872 moved and rebuilt here, and the floating collection includes Spartan, Scotland's last Scottish-built puffer, the tug Garnock and the 1898 steam yacht Carola. The Harbour Arts Centre rounds out the waterfront draw.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Beach Park, the long stretch of dune and sand laid out around the harbourside. Eglinton Country Park, over 400 hectares of the former Eglinton Estate, offers walking, cycling, horse riding and fishing, while the Magnum at Beach Park has long served as the area's swimming, ice and indoor sports hub. Indoor boating ponds at the museum and the estuary trails keep families busy through the season.

Heritage and culture run through the old royal burgh and its festival calendar. The Marymass Festival, a medieval horse festival led by the Irvine Carters' Society since 1753, fills twelve August days with horse racing, jousting, parades and the crowning of the Marymass Queen. The harbourside streets, the Glasgow Vennel where Robert Burns once lived and worked, and the year-round arts programme give the town a distinct historic character.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base across the town and along the coast toward Troon and Ayr, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching out to the Isle of Arran ferry at Ardrossan. Irvine station and the bus links to Kilmarnock, Ayr, Greenock and Glasgow bring visitors in, and Glasgow Prestwick Airport sits a short hop south, so operators here handle seasonal coastal trade and stopover crowds alike.

Aberdare.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Cynon Valley
s1loc: Aberdare anchors the Cynon Valley visitor economy at the head of the South Wales valleys. The Cynon Valley Museum tells the area's industrial and arts story, while St Elvan's Church, a Grade II-star listed Anglican church of 1851, and the Iron Tram Bridge at Robertstown, an early railway bridge over the River Cynon, mark the town's mining and tramroad past. Aberdare Market Hall, built in 1853, hosted the first National Eisteddfod of the modern era in 1861.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Dare Valley Country Park, 500 acres of woodland, pasture and moorland in a glacial valley just west of the town. The park holds the Gravity Family Bike Park and pump track, over 200 acres of trails, an adventure playground, lakes for canoe and kayak hire and the Dare Valley Trout Fishery. Aberdare Park, a 50-acre Victorian green space with rose gardens, adds gentler walks above the valley.

Heritage and culture run through Trecynon and the town centre. The Coliseum Theatre, a 1930s art deco venue with a 600-seat auditorium and cinema, runs a year-round programme of drama, music, comedy and seasonal pantomime, and the town keeps a calendar of festive markets and commemorative events. The former collieries at Cwmdare and the wider valley landscape give walkers and heritage visitors a strong sense of industrial south Wales.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and inn base across the valley, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching out to the Brecon Beacons and Penderyn Distillery just to the north. Aberdare station on the Valley Lines puts Cardiff within easy reach, and the A4059 carries visitors up onto the moorland and over toward Brecon, so operators here handle seasonal walking and outdoor trade alongside town-centre and market crowds.

Lichfield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Lichfield cathedral city
s1loc: Lichfield draws a steady cathedral-city visitor economy in southern Staffordshire, crowned by Lichfield Cathedral, the only medieval three-spired cathedral in the country, its trio known as the Ladies of the Vale. Over 1,300 years of history sit inside, from the Herkenrode stained glass and the Lichfield Gospels of 730 to the Lichfield Angel of 700, with tower tours giving views across the surrounding countryside and the historic Cathedral Close around it.

The leisure and activity layer spreads out around the town. Beacon Park, a large landscaped green space beside the Cathedral Close, offers play areas, boating and the Museum Gardens, while Stowe Pool and Minster Pool give walkers water-side circuits in the heart of the city. The National Memorial Arboretum at nearby Alrewas, with its 150 acres and thousands of trees, draws coach trade and family visits across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run deep in the birthplace of Samuel Johnson. The Samuel Johnson Birthplace Museum on the market square, the Erasmus Darwin House and the Lichfield Heritage galleries anchor the historic offer, while the Garrick Theatre stages drama and the annual Lichfield Festival fills July with concerts and events in the cathedral and across the city. The medieval streets and the Friary precinct give the centre a distinct historic character year-round.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade across the city and out toward the A38, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around the cathedral and the arboretum. Lichfield City and Lichfield Trent Valley stations and the M6 Toll bring day-trippers from Birmingham and beyond, with Cannock Chase, the National Forest and the country houses of the county a short trip out for visitors based in the city.

Letchworth.region: Letchworth Garden City and north Hertfordshire
Letchworth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Hertfordshire
s1loc: Letchworth carries a distinctive heritage visitor economy as the world's first Garden City, laid out from 1903 to Ebenezer Howard's plan. The International Garden Cities Exhibition tells that founding story, while the Arts and Crafts landmarks of the Spirella Building, a restored former corsetry factory, and the Cloisters draw architecture enthusiasts. The Broadway Gallery and the planned avenues of the town centre give visitors a townscape unlike anywhere else in the country.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Standalone Farm, a working farm on the Garden City Greenway where families meet the animals and learn rural skills. The Greenway itself rings the town on a 13-mile walking and cycling route, while Howard Park and Gardens offers a children's splash park and Broadway Gardens its splendid fountain. Norton Common, a large area of semi-natural woodland and meadow, gives walkers green space close to the centre.

Heritage and culture centre on the art deco Broadway Cinema and Theatre, a striking 1936 building showing films and staging shows for all ages on the town square. The Garden City heritage trail, the Broadway Gallery exhibitions and the town's events calendar keep the cultural offer busy through the year, while the surrounding conservation areas and Arts and Crafts housing give guides a rich subject across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and hotel base serving heritage visitors and business trade, with a guide scene built around the Garden City story. Letchworth Garden City station puts London King's Cross within easy reach and links the town to Cambridge, while the A1(M) brings day-trippers in, with the Chilterns, Hitchin's market and the countryside of north Hertfordshire a short trip out for visitors based in the town.

Haywards Heath.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Mid Sussex
s1loc: Haywards Heath sits at the centre of Mid Sussex, a market and commuter town whose draw is its parks and gardens and the wider Wealden countryside. Beech Hurst Gardens, a heritage park on the town's edge, has held the Green Flag award for years running and offers a miniature railway, croquet lawn and bowling strip among its landscaped grounds. The town serves as a base for the South Downs and the famous gardens of the surrounding district.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Victoria Park, a large green space with a children's playground, outdoor water play, a skate park, tennis courts and football pitches. Clair Park near the station holds a cricket pitch and a weekly parkrun within its woodland setting, while the Dolphin Leisure Centre adds a swimming pool, squash courts and a sports hall, keeping families and activity operators busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on Clair Hall, the town's entertainment and events venue beside the station, which runs a programme of shows and community events through the year. The conservation streets of the old Muster Green, the parish church of St Wilfrid and the surrounding Wealden villages give the town a quiet historic character, with the events calendar and the parks hosting fairs and gatherings across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base serving business and leisure trade, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the South Downs and the gardens of Sussex. Haywards Heath station puts London under an hour away on the Brighton main line and links the town to Gatwick, so operators here handle stopover and commuter trade as well as visitors heading for Wakehurst, Borde Hill and the coast nearby. Beech Hurst Gardens, Victoria Park and Clair Park sit in the town, with the Ardingly showground and Sheffield Park close by.

Uxbridge.region: Uxbridge and the London Borough of Hillingdon
Uxbridge.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west London and Hillingdon
s1loc: Uxbridge anchors a west London visitor economy in the London Borough of Hillingdon, led by the Battle of Britain Bunker. The Exhibition and Visitor Centre houses RAF Fighter Command's No.11 Group Operations Room, the underground room from which most of the RAF's side of the Battle of Britain was co-ordinated and where Churchill spoke his famous words about the few. A tour drops 76 steps to the original 1940s bunker before the museum displays above.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the Colne Valley Regional Park, a mosaic of farmland, woodland and water with over 70 lakes and 200 kilometres of river and canal stretching from Rickmansworth to the Thames. The Colne Valley Park Visitor Centre and Riverside Cafe, the lakeside trails and watersports, and Ruislip Lido with its miniature railway and woods give families and activity operators green space and water close to the town.

Heritage and culture run along the Grand Union Canal, which threads through the valley past Uxbridge Lock and Cowley Lock with its flat, paved towpath and lock-side history. The town's old market house, the Crown and Treaty inn where Civil War peace talks were held, and the events calendar around the canal and the bunker give guides plenty to work with, with seasonal trips and walks filling the warmer months.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-apartment base serving business and airport trade, with a guide scene built around the bunker and the canal. Uxbridge sits at the end of the Metropolitan and Piccadilly lines into central London, the A40 and M40 run west toward Oxford, and Heathrow lies just to the south, so operators here handle airport stopover crowds, business visitors and day-trippers across the year.
